description:
Microsoft has launched Decision-1, an AI model that returns probabilities for predefined answers, allowing software applications to use its outputs directly instead of processing a free-form response from a large language model (LLM).

The model targets tasks such as classifying requests, prioritizing incidents, and checking AI-generated responses. Microsoft says it can handle these decisions with lower costs and latency than approaches that rely on general-purpose LLMs.

“Instead of writing a free-form response, it takes a fixed set of answer options and returns a calibrated probability for each
title: Microsoft separates decision-making from generative AI with a new model

description: Developers have never been more inclined to use AI, yet never less inclined to trust its output. In Stack Overflow’s surveys, the proportion of respondents using AI tools in development keeps climbing (44% in 2023, 62% in 2024, and 83% in 2026), but trust hasn’t kept pace. In the 2025 accuracy question, only about 33% trusted AI’s output, while 46% distrusted it. In 2026 Stack Overflow changed the question but still found only 7% of developers trust AI with important work decisions, rising to 48% if they can eas
title: AI distrust is GitHub’s opportunity

description: Every new laptop today is marketed as an ‘AI PC’ thanks to a built-in Neural Processing Unit (NPU). But beyond chatting with small local LLMs, what practical work can this silicon actually do? Recently, I hit a wall with a classic IT problem: data gravity. I had about a hundred gigabytes of scanned family photos that needed to be organized and enhanced. Uploading gigabytes of media to a cloud AI API for something as straightforward as deduplication is unreasonable. The compute needed to move to the data, and that meant putting my laptop’s idle NPU to work. Source code for the scripts used in this article is available on GitHub.
title: Local AI on NPUs: Building a zero-cloud photo deduplicator with OpenCLIP

description: During my tenure as InfoWorld’s blogger-in-chief I became fascinated with narrated videos of software in action. Tools existed to do that kind of storytelling but the explanatory power of what came to be called screencasting had not yet been widely recognized. Although the medium became a standard way to demonstrate software, and I went on to produce and edit many screencasts over the years, the available tools never worked the way I wanted them to: easy and precise frame-accurate previewing and execution of annotations, cuts, pauses
title: Screencasting in the AI era

description: Every few weeks, another enterprise leader asks me the same question: Should our AI agents run in the cloud or in our own data center? It sounds like a simple either/or, but it is the wrong way to frame the decision. Agents are not a single workload. They are orchestrated collections of model inference, tool execution, memory state, and integration logic. Some pieces belong in the cloud, some belong on-premises, and the failure mode I see repeatedly is choosing a location by ideology or from a vendor’s sales deck rather than by the characteristics of each agent
title: The best place to run AI agents
